Voice Leading Triads: Practice for Chapter 26

Chapter 26 of Hutchinson’s Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom: SATB part writing with triads, parallels, ranges, spacing, doubling in each inversion and the six-four chords, with checked examples and exercises marked by a voice-leading checker.

This page goes with Chapter 26, Voice Leading Triads of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first; the book is the reference for the rules. It builds on Chapter 6, Triads, Chapter 7, Roman Numerals and Chapter 16, Figured Bass.

How the page works. Each example is drawn on a grand staff (soprano and alto on the treble staff, tenor and bass below), plays when you press Play, and is marked by a checker: the same program that marks your exercises. A green Right is an example the checker passes, a red Wrong one shows what the checker says about it. In the exercises the bass (and sometimes the soprano) is given; type the other notes (E4, F#4, Bb3; Up and Down move a step in the key) and press Check.

26.1 What voice leading is

Voice leading (part writing) is the set of rules for how each voice moves from one chord to the next. Four things matter: each part should be independent, each chord should be voiced well, the parts should move economically, and each part should be singable. SATB (chorale style) puts soprano, alto, tenor and bass on two staves; piano style puts the upper three voices in the treble staff and the bass alone in the bass staff. The model is Bach’s chorales.

Two voices move in one of four ways: contrary (opposite directions), oblique (one holds, the other moves), similar (same direction) and parallel (same direction by the same interval, a kind of similar motion).

26.2 Objectionable parallels

Do not write parallel fifths or parallel octaves (or their compound forms, twelfths and unisons) between any two voices: they make two voices sound like one. Parallel 3rds, 4ths and 6ths are fine; parallel 2nds and 7ths are rarely used.

Fifths and octaves do not move in parallel here: the soprano and alto hold the common tone C and the bass leaps.
Parallel fifths: the tenor and bass both rise a step and keep a perfect fifth (G to C, then A to D).
Parallel octaves: the soprano and bass both rise a step, octave to octave.

26.3 Voice ranges

Keep each voice in the range of the book’s figure: soprano D4 to F#5, alto G3 to C#5, tenor E♭3 to F#4, bass E2 to C4. (These are narrower than real voices on purpose; the figure was read off the staff and the checker uses it as written.)

The soprano’s G5 is above the range.

26.4 Rules of melody

Every voice is a melody. The book’s rules, from Bach’s practice: tendency tones resolve (7 up to 8, and, less strictly, 4 down to 3; 6 and 2 fall); avoid augmented intervals; a leap larger than a 4th, or a diminished leap, changes direction afterwards; and consecutive leaps outline a triad. The checker flags the first two always (the leap rule as an error in the upper voices and a warning in the bass) and warns about two leaps in the same direction that do not outline a triad.

26.5 Spacing, crossing and overlap

Keep soprano and alto, and alto and tenor, within an octave of each other. More is a spacing error; the tenor and bass may be farther apart. Two more faults belong with independence of parts (the names are this site’s): voice crossing, a voice below the voice under it, and overlap, a voice moving past where its neighbour has just been.

The alto (G4) and tenor (E3) are more than an octave apart.
The alto is above the soprano.
The alto leaps to B3, below the tenor’s C4 of a moment ago (and across it).

26.6 Root position triads in four parts

A triad has three notes and there are four voices, so one is doubled. In root position, double the root (that is, the bass). Then look at how the bass moves:

Bass moves by Upper three voices
a 3rd or 6th keep both common tones, move the third voice by step
a 4th or 5th keep one common tone and move the other two by step, or move all three the same way to the nearest chord tones
a 2nd move all three upper voices in contrary motion to the bass
the same note repeated keep the upper voices or rearrange them, keeping root, third and fifth
Bass down a 3rd (I to vi): two common tones (E, C), the soprano moves up a step.
I IV V I: a 4th up (one common tone), a 2nd up (the upper voices fall, contrary to the bass), a 5th down (one common tone).

The deceptive progression. When V goes to vi (VI in minor) the bass rises a 2nd, so the upper voices would fall, but the leading tone must rise. The book’s answer: move the third of V up by step and the other two voices down, so the third of vi is doubled. In major, do the same only if 7 is in the soprano.

V to vi: the leading tone (tenor) rises to C, the others fall; the third of vi is doubled.
The leading tone in the soprano (B4) must rise to C; it leaps down to G.
The leading tone (the third of V) is doubled: never do that.
A root position triad doubles the root; here the fifth is doubled and the root only sounds in the bass.

26.7 First inversion triads

Now the bass is the third, so look at the doubling instead of the bass distance. Do not double the bass of a first inversion triad: double the root or the fifth, whichever moves most smoothly. Exceptions: a diminished triad in first inversion (such as vii°6) doubles the third (the bass), and in a run of first inversion chords the third is doubled in every other chord. Never double the third of V (it is the leading tone).

I6 doubles the root (C), not the bass; the soprano rises a step, the tenor falls to the leading tone.
The bass E (the third) is doubled in a major first inversion triad.
A diminished first inversion triad doubles its third (the bass, D); here the fifth F is doubled.
The figure 6 means the third is in the bass; the bass has the root.

26.8 Second inversion triads and the six-four chord

Double the bass (the fifth of the chord) in a second inversion triad. There are three places a six-four chord is used:

  • Cadential: I64 to V, the 6 and 4 above the bass falling to 5 and 3 (the sixth resolves to the fifth, the fourth to the third).
  • Pedal (or neighbor): I IV64 I, or V I64 V: the bass holds while the upper voices move.
  • Passing: I V64 I6, or IV I64 IV6: the bass walks through by step.
Cadential six-four: the bass G is doubled; E falls to D and C falls to B.
Pedal six-four: the bass holds C while the upper voices move to IV and back.
In a six-four chord the bass (the fifth) is doubled; here only the bass has G.

Special situation: roots a second apart. When two chords have roots a 2nd apart (IV to V, ii to I6), avoid parallel fifths by voicing each chord with the fifth below the root in the upper voices.

26.9 Exercises

One. Bass given: I IV V I. Add soprano, alto and tenor: double the root in each chord, keep common tones where the bass moves by a 4th or 5th, move contrary where it moves by a 2nd.

Two. Soprano and bass given, with a vi. The bass rises and falls by 3rds and 2nds.

Three. A first inversion chord. In I6 double the root or the fifth; the soprano resolves the leading tone in the last bar.

Four. Minor. In A minor the leading tone is G♯; write it as G#.

NoteWhat the checker does and does not check
  • It marks ranges, spacing, crossing, overlap, parallel fifths and octaves, the leading tone (doubled, or not resolved), the doubling for each chord position, complete chords and the melodic rules above. Rule by rule, with the chapter each comes from, they are listed in the header of apps/shared/analysis/voice-leading.js.
  • Site’s readings: the exact notes of the ranges (read off the book’s figure), the names crossing and overlap, direct fifths and octaves in the outer voices (a warning: the book states that rule only for species counterpoint), and “no fifth only with the root tripled”.
  • Not checked: consecutive thirds and sixths, the “roots a second apart” voicing, the Mozart K. 331 exception, and whether the Roman numerals suit a melody. A clean result means no rule above is broken; it does not mean the music is good.
  • The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
